analysis.one_liner: Requires electricity suppliers nationwide to meet a federal renewable electricity standard.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2026 and referred to the Senate Energy Committee, where it has sat with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require retail electricity suppliers across the country to get a share of their power from renewable sources like wind and solar, under a federal standard added to a 1978 utility law. Today, renewable requirements exist state by state; this would make them national and mandatory. The bill was introduced by Senator Peter Welch with one cosponsor and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which has not acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people would benefit over time from a cleaner, potentially cheaper long-run electricity mix and reduced air pollution from fossil plants, since the standard applies to the electricity everyone uses. The renewable energy industry gains a guaranteed nationwide market for wind and solar generation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households that use electricity; renewable energy firms

how_it_helps.text: It would require retail electricity suppliers nationwide to meet a federal renewable electricity standard, replacing a patchwork of state-level rules with a single national floor.
A national renewable standard would reduce the share of electricity generated from fossil fuels, the main source of American power-plant carbon emissions.

analysis.who_pays: Utilities that burn coal and gas would pay to buy renewable power or generate it themselves, and some of that cost would flow to ratepayers — especially in states with little renewable capacity. Fossil fuel industries would lose electricity market share.

drawbacks.text: A federal mandate on retail electricity suppliers could raise electricity prices in regions that depend on fossil fuels, and those costs fall on ordinary households — the bill's text does not detail how compliance costs would be cushioned.
The bill has a single cosponsor and sits in a committee whose majority is not aligned with its sponsor, so the policy may never receive a serious hearing, let alone a floor vote.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a nationwide shift to renewable electricity — could lower emissions and eventually steady electricity costs, but the bill as introduced is unproven and faces steep odds: it has one cosponsor, a committee with a Republican majority, and a Congress that has not advanced comparable standards. The cost of doing nothing is continued fossil-fuel dependence, but whether this particular design can pass — and at what cost to consumers in fossil-heavy states — is unresolved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which has taken no action on it; the bill has not received a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 17, 2026, and read twice before being referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote.
The bill has one cosponsor, a Democratic senator.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil-fired electricity suppliers and the utilities that rely on them are better off so far, since no federal standard has moved. The bill's fate rests with the Energy and Natural Resources Committee and Senate leadership, neither of which has acted on it.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a federal renewable electricity standard.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsors are both Democrats, and with Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats, a federal renewable standard has no visible path without Republican support, none of which appears in the record.

industries.industry: Wind, solar, and other renewable electricity producers
industries.note: A federal renewable electricity standard creates guaranteed nationwide demand for renewable generation, giving these industries a stable, legally required market.

industries.industry: Coal- and gas-fired electric utilities and fuel suppliers
industries.note: A renewable standard forces them to buy more renewable power or retire fossil generation, cutting into their existing share of electricity sales. Their interest runs against cheaper-to-run fossil plants that utilities and consumers currently rely on.

Households would pay whatever compliance requires, though renewables often carry low and stable operating costs once built. The outcome depends entirely on the standard's details, which the summary does not provide.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor, no committee action months out, and a Republican majority on the Energy Committee, the bill is very likely to die in committee when this Congress ends in January 2027, as most such proposals do.
